Expectations were low heading into COP31. But at the very least, it was anticipated that Türkiye, the host nation, and Australia in its role of President of Negotiations would deliver some form of consensus on tackling climate change. Even this low bar wasn’t achieved.
Talks on the proposed Antalya Pact had begun with some promise. Targets for achieving 35% electrification of final energy by 2035, agreeing just transition provisions, tripling climate finance and deploying carbon capture and storage technologies seemed realistic. But deep divisions around the text to “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” proved unbridgeable, despite protracted negotiations. The result was no consensus and no final draft, and the first COP since 2009 to conclude without a core agreement. 
I asked VP Prakash Sharma and our Energy Transition team for their initial thoughts.
First, mounting challenges this decade have progressively weakened the collective resolve to tackle global warming. 
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order, trade disputes and ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran have elevated energy security above climate change as many governments’ primary focus. 
Fossil fuels remain the backbone of the energy system in virtually all countries, meeting 80% of global energy demand. Eleven years on from the Paris Agreement, it is (almost) universally acknowledged that transitioning to a low-carbon energy system can’t happen overnight, especially with global demand rising faster than supply. Supply disruptions and spiralling oil and LNG prices triggered by the Iran war may have underlined the vulnerability of countries that depend heavily on imported hydrocarbons, but neither has fundamentally changed the outlook.   
Second, resource-rich oil and gas exporters are on the front foot.
An acceleration of electrification, most likely to take hold in oil and gas importing countries, threatens their economic future. 
Fossil fuel producers seized their opportunity in Antalya. By keeping any reference to phasing out fossil fuels from the final text, producers sidestepped any renewed impetus to the goals of the Paris Agreement. With or without those words, the reality is that fossil fuels will continue to play a critical part in energy security for decades to come as we forecast in our Energy Transition Outlook earlier this month.
Ultimately, what matters is competitiveness. Renewables, competitive in most power markets, will continue to grow along with other low-carbon technologies, not least batteries and electric vehicles. Oil and gas at current elevated prices can’t compete, but our expectation is that prices could soon fall – and sharply. And with power demand rising at pace due to data centres, electric vehicles and advanced manufacturing, some countries may take a pragmatic view, soften their anti-fossil fuels stance and allow the current energy mix to persist.    
Third, some oil and gas importers – Europe included – may actually benefit from the omission of the text on fossil fuels. 
While Europe is at the vanguard of climate policy and decarbonisation, it remains a major importer of oil and gas. Moreover, some European countries, including the UK, are in a quandary over whether to approve new investment in domestic production. The failure of talks in Antalya may smooth the path for these governments to greenlight new upstream projects.  
Fourth, there is a global leadership vacuum on tackling climate change. 
The absence of the US from both COP30 and COP31 has undoubtedly weakened the ability to achieve consensus. The Democratic party has signalled its intention to take the US back into the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, but even with majorities in both chambers of Congress following this month’s midterms, it will take victory in the 2028 presidential election for this to become a realistic prospect. With affordability top of the political agenda, curtailing investment in oil and gas doesn’t look a vote winner. 
China, meanwhile, has chosen not to grasp a climate leadership role that was there for the taking. Its position as the global pacesetter in manufacturing and exporting low-carbon technologies and dominance of critical minerals for the transition may be proving a sufficient prize. 
Leadership and cooperation are essential if multilateral climate goals are to be achieved. The lack of consensus on display at COP31, however, is further evidence of the growing failure of global institutions to act decisively on areas such as climate, conflict and trade. 
Belief in the ability of future COPs to deliver global action is now wafer-thin: without consensus, countries will increasingly have little option but to determine their own futures.
